mercy_translation.text:
Who among those testified to in Scripture had hands and feet pierced, or was hung upon wood and perfected on a cross for the salvation of all? Abraham died lying on a bed. Isaac and Jacob also drew up their feet and died upon beds. Moses and Aaron died on the mountain; David died in his house, suffering no plot from the people. Though Saul hunted him, he was preserved unharmed. Isaiah was sawn, but he was not hung upon wood. Jeremiah was insulted but did not die under condemnation. Ezekiel suffered, but not on behalf of the people; rather, he signified what would happen to the people.

Moreover, these people, even when they suffered, were human beings like all others according to the likeness of nature. But the One indicated by the Scriptures as suffering on behalf of all is called not merely a human being but the Life of all, although like human beings according to nature. For it says, “You shall see your Life hanging before your eyes,” and, “Who shall describe his generation?” One may learn and recount the lineage of all the saints—who each one was and from where he came. But concerning the One who is Life, the divine words declare his generation to be beyond narration.

Who, then, is the One about whom the divine Scriptures say these things? Who is so great that the prophets proclaimed so much beforehand concerning him? No one else is found in the Scriptures except the common Savior of all, the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the One who came forth from a virgin, appeared as a human being on earth, and has an indescribable generation according to the flesh. For no one can name a human father of his body, since his body was not from a man but from a virgin alone.

Just as one can trace the fathers of David, Moses, and all the patriarchs, so no one can recount the Savior's bodily generation from a man. He is the One who caused the star to signify the birth of his body. For it was fitting that the Word who came down from heaven should have his sign from heaven; and it was fitting that the King of creation, when he came forth, should be made manifest to the whole inhabited world.

Indeed, he was born in Judea, and people from Persia came to worship him. He is the One who even before his bodily manifestation won victory over the opposing demons and trophies over idolatry. For people from the nations everywhere renounce ancestral customs and the godlessness of idols, place their hope in Christ, and enroll themselves under him—as one can see with one's own eyes.

Never did the godlessness of the Egyptians cease except when the Lord of all, as though riding upon a cloud, descended there in the body, abolished the error of idols, and transferred everyone to himself and through himself to the Father.

He is the One crucified with the sun, creation, and even those who brought death upon him as witnesses. By his death salvation came to all and all creation was redeemed. He is the Life of all, and like a sheep he handed over his own body to death as a life in exchange for all, for the salvation of all—even though the Jews do not believe.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius identifies Christ with the prophetic figure whose death, lineage, and universal significance surpass those of earlier biblical figures.
The phrase 'life in exchange for all' renders Athanasius' representative sacrificial language without importing later formulations.
